# Purpose of this document

This document is a complete technical handoff for turning the working pipeline in this
repository into a proper installable package. It covers: what the pipeline does, why
every design choice was made (with the actual measured evidence behind it), what data
format is required and how to get it, and — critically — a full log of what was already
tried and rejected, so none of that work gets silently repeated.

The three production scripts already in `models/` (`gcn_gae_improved_model.py`,
`gcn_gae_bilinear_model.py`, `gcn_gae_ensemble_best_model.py`) are working reference
implementations. This document explains the reasoning behind them well enough that a
package can be built around the same logic, restructured properly (modules, tests,
config, CLI), without needing to re-derive any of the validated decisions from scratch.

# Project overview

**Goal:** reconstruct a Gene Regulatory Network (GRN) — which genes regulate which other
genes — by combining the outputs of many different existing GRN-inference algorithms
through a Graph Convolutional Network Graph Autoencoder (GCN-GAE), rather than trusting
any single algorithm alone.

**Core idea:** each individual inference algorithm (correlation-based, mutual-information-
based, tree-ensemble-based, etc.) captures a different, partial view of the true
regulatory structure, and each has its own blind spots and false positives. Feeding each
algorithm's output through its own trained GCN encoder, then combining (fusing) all of
the encoders' reconstructions together, recovers a more accurate, more complete network
than any single algorithm — including edges no single algorithm proposed on its own (the
GCN can "discover" links that weren't in its own input, because it's learning latent
structure, not just copying the input graph).

**Validated result:** on DREAM4 benchmark networks (100-gene synthetic networks with
known ground truth), this approach beats both the best individual algorithm (GENIE3
variants) and GENECI's own evolutionary-optimized ensemble method on AUPR (the priority
metric, given the ~3.5% true-edge class imbalance in this kind of problem), and on AUROC
for 2 of the 3 networks tested.

# GENECI: what it is, and how we use it

## What GENECI is

[GENECI](https://github.com/AdrianSeguraOrtiz/GENECI) is an open-source tool
(Segura-Ortiz et al.) that runs a large collection of established GRN-inference
algorithms against a gene expression dataset. It supports 26 total techniques, spanning
several different methodological families:

- **Mutual-information / correlation-based:** ARACNE, BC3NET, C3NET, CLR, MRNET, MRNETB,
  PCIT
- **Tree-ensemble / boosting-based:** GENIE3 (both Extra-Trees and Random-Forest
  variants), GRNBOOST2, KBOOST
- **Regression-based:** TIGRESS, INFERELATOR
- **Other / distinct methodology:** LEAP, NONLINEARODES, MEOMI, JUMP3, NARROMI, CMI2NI,
  RSNET, PCACMI, LOCPCACMI, PLSNET, PIDC, PUC, GRNVBEM

GENECI also has its own downstream ensemble-optimization step
(`geneci optimize-ensemble`), which uses an evolutionary algorithm to find optimal
per-algorithm weights and produce one consensus network. **This project does not use that
step.** Only the individual algorithm-inference step is used — see below.

## How we actually use it

We run **only** GENECI's `infer-network` command, which executes each requested
algorithm independently against the expression data and writes out each algorithm's own
raw, continuous confidence scores. We do not run `optimize-ensemble` — the combination
of algorithm outputs is done entirely by our own GCN-GAE pipeline, not GENECI's built-in
evolutionary method.

Example command (16 of the 26 available techniques; the other 10 — JUMP3, NARROMI,
CMI2NI, RSNET, PCACMI, LOCPCACMI, PLSNET, PIDC, PUC, GRNVBEM — are available but were not
part of the original test set; they can be added the same way):

```
geneci infer-network --expression-data path/to/expression_data.csv \
                     --technique ARACNE --technique BC3NET --technique C3NET \
                     --technique CLR --technique GENIE3_RF --technique GRNBOOST2 \
                     --technique GENIE3_ET --technique MRNET --technique MRNETB \
                     --technique PCIT --technique TIGRESS --technique KBOOST \
                     --technique MEOMI --technique LEAP --technique NONLINEARODES \
                     --technique INFERELATOR \
                     --output-dir inferred_networks
```

This produces one folder per dataset (e.g. `inferred_networks/<dataset_name>/`),
containing a `lists/` subfolder with one file per algorithm:

```
inferred_networks/<dataset_name>/lists/GRN_ARACNE.csv
inferred_networks/<dataset_name>/lists/GRN_CLR.csv
inferred_networks/<dataset_name>/lists/GRN_GENIE3_ET.csv
... (one per requested technique)
```

Each of these files is a **3-column edge list**, no header:
`source_gene,target_gene,confidence_score` — continuous scores in `[0, 1]`, one row per
gene pair the algorithm considered non-negligible (pairs it didn't list are implicitly
zero).

## Critical gotcha already discovered — do not repeat this mistake

GENECI (or an earlier step in this project's original data-prep pipeline) also produces
files named like `normalized_weight_matrix_all_GRN_<dataset>_<filter>.csv`, in a wide
matrix format (one row/column block per algorithm). **These files are already
pre-binarized** — every single value in them is exactly `0` or `1`, despite the
"normalized_weight_matrix" name suggesting continuous values. This was discovered the
hard way, after an entire day of threshold-sweep experiments produced suspiciously
identical results across different threshold values (0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 all gave
identical edge counts) — the values simply had no continuous gradation left to
threshold.

**Always use the raw `lists/GRN_<ALGORITHM>.csv` files from GENECI's `infer-network`
output directly. Never use the `normalized_weight_matrix_*.csv` files as the continuous
score source.**

# Full pipeline, step by step

## Step 1 — Load real continuous per-algorithm scores

Read each `GRN_<ALGORITHM>.csv` edge list, reconstruct a full `(num_genes, num_genes)`
matrix per algorithm (unlisted pairs = 0). This is implemented in
`load_algorithm_matrices()` in the production scripts.

## Step 2 — Build per-algorithm input topology (top-X% rank-based threshold)

For each algorithm, independently: rank all gene pairs by that algorithm's own
confidence score, and keep the **top 10%** as edges for that algorithm's graph. This
decides the topology the GCN encoder trains on for that algorithm — nothing else about
the raw scores is used at this stage (the actual confidence values are discarded once
topology is decided, unless native-weight edge confidence is enabled — see below).

### Why top-10%, and why rank-based rather than a fixed score cutoff

A fixed absolute score cutoff (the original pipeline used `0.6`, later `0.15`) is
fundamentally not comparable across 16 different algorithms, because each algorithm
produces scores on a completely different internal scale. **Measured evidence:** at a
fixed cutoff of `0.6`, `GRN_LEAP` alone kept ~67% of all possible gene pairs as edges,
while several other algorithms kept under 0.3% — the same absolute number meant wildly
different things per algorithm.

Switching to a **rank-based** cutoff ("keep each algorithm's own top X%") fixes the
cross-algorithm comparability problem. The specific value of X was chosen with the
following logic, validated on DREAM4 (real evidence, not a guess):

- A sweep across X in {5, 10, 15, 20, 30, ...}% showed a broad stable AUROC/AUPR plateau
  in roughly the 5-20% range, with a sharp performance cliff beyond ~20-30%.
- Reframed against each DREAM4 network's own *known* true regulatory density (3.5-5%
  across the 3 networks tested), the validated 10% setting corresponds to roughly
  **2-3x each network's own true density** — not an arbitrary percentage, but a
  multiplier on expected network sparsity.
- This mirrors the precedent set in the original GENIE3 paper (Huynh-Thu et al., 2010),
  which explicitly could not find a principled absolute threshold and instead
  recommended matching the predicted network's edge count to a known/expected true
  count when one is available. We extend that logic with a 2-3x safety margin, since
  this threshold controls *input topology* for further learning, not the final answer.
- **For real biological data with no known ground truth** (e.g. a new organism), the
  equivalent, defensible approach is to use an **independent, literature-based estimate**
  of that organism's expected regulatory network density (e.g. RegulonDB's documented
  TF-target statistics for E. coli), and apply the same validated 2-3x multiplier — never
  tuning X against the actual unknown ground truth for the dataset being analyzed.
- **Caveat:** the "10%" value itself, and the "2-3x" multiplier, have only been validated
  across 3 DREAM4 networks from the same synthetic-network-generation family. Whether the
  multiplier itself transfers to a different organism (E. coli) is an open, high-priority
  validation item — see Open Items below.

## Step 3 — Encode: 3-layer GCN

```
Encoder architecture (validated, do not change without re-testing):
  Input (identity matrix, num_genes x num_genes) 
    -> GCNConv -> 32 channels -> ReLU
    -> GCNConv -> 32 channels -> BatchNorm -> ReLU -> Dropout(0.01) -> +residual
    -> GCNConv -> 16 channels (final embedding) -> ReLU
```

Node features are the **identity matrix** (each gene is just a one-hot ID vector, no
expression values). This was deliberately tested against using real gene expression
values as node features, and identity clearly won — using expression values as node
features made every metric worse, even with more training. The reasoning: identity
features force the GCN to learn embeddings purely from graph topology, which turns out
to be well-matched to what a graph-autoencoder reconstruction task rewards; injecting a
different signal (expression) distracted from that rather than helping.

Depth (3 layers) and width `(32, 32, 16)` were both validated against several
alternatives — see the rejected-experiments table below. Nothing tested beat this shape.

## Step 4 — Decode: bilinear + distance decoder ensemble

The current best-validated decoder is actually **two decoders, trained separately, with
their outputs averaged together**:

**Bilinear decoder:** `score = sigmoid(z_i^T W z_j)`, where `W` is a learned matrix,
initialized near the identity matrix. This is the key upgrade over a plain inner-product
decoder (`z_i . z_j`), which is mathematically forced to be symmetric
(`z_i.z_j == z_j.z_i`) and therefore cannot represent directional regulation (a
transcription factor regulating a target gene is not the same relationship in reverse).
With a learned `W`, `z_i^T W z_j != z_j^T W z_i` in general.

**Distance decoder:** `score = sigmoid(-||z_i - z_j||^2)` — a completely different idea
(proximity in embedding space, rather than a learned interaction matrix).

**Why ensemble the two:** each decoder alone beat the original plain inner-product
decoder, but neither was consistently the single best option across all 3 DREAM4
networks tested. Averaging their outputs together beat *both* individual decoders on
AUPR on every network tested, and beat both on AUROC on 2 of 3 networks — the most
consistent result found across the whole architecture-testing process, more consistent
than either decoder alone.

## Step 5 — Train

- 300 epochs (raised from an original 150 — every decoder alternative tested showed real
  further gains with more training that 150 epochs was under-selling)
- Adam optimizer, learning rate `0.01`, weight decay `1e-8`
- Standard GAE reconstruction loss (binary cross-entropy between predicted edge
  probability and actual edge/non-edge, with automatic random negative sampling from
  non-edges)
- 3 independent training runs ("iterations") per algorithm per decoder, to average out
  random-initialization noise

## Step 6 — Fuse

**Continuous averaging** — take every trained model's raw `[0,1]`-normalized continuous
reconstruction (16 algorithms x 3 iterations x 2 decoders = 96 individual reconstructions
in the full ensemble pipeline) and average them all together, element-wise, into one
final continuous adjacency matrix.

**Do not binarize before combining.** The original pipeline binarized each individual
run's output, then summed those binary matrices into a vote count, then thresholded the
vote count. Continuous averaging was tested against this on identical trained models
(same training runs, only the combination method differed) and produced a real ~0.02
AUROC improvement — binarizing early throws away exactly how confident each prediction
was, which continuous averaging preserves all the way through.

## Optional Step 7 — Final network extraction (if a specific edge list is needed)

The continuous fused matrix is a *ranking*, not a final yes/no answer. If a specific
final list of predicted edges is needed (rather than a continuous score for every gene
pair), a real, principled option was validated: **Tukey's IQR outlier rule (Tukey,
1977)** — the same standard convention that draws the whiskers on a boxplot — applied
per-gene:

```
for each gene's own row of connection scores:
    Q1, Q3 = 25th and 75th percentile of that gene's own scores
    IQR = Q3 - Q1
    keep connections where score > Q3 + k*IQR
```

`k=1.5` ("mild outlier") or `k=3.0` ("extreme outlier") are both standard, citable
values — no tuning against ground truth required. Which one to use depends on which
decoder produced the continuous scores (see validated numbers below) — the right k is
not universal across decoders, since it depends on the shape of that decoder's score
distribution, not an arbitrary choice.

**Important: never compute AUROC/AUPR on the post-cutoff binary network.** These metrics
are computed on the continuous score, before any cutoff is applied, and will always look
worse if computed after — that's not the method failing, it's what these metrics
structurally measure (ranking quality across every possible cutoff, not one committed
decision). Report AUROC/AUPR on the pre-cutoff continuous score, and report
precision/recall/F1 separately for the actual final network the cutoff produces.

# Validated design choices (reference table)

| Component | Choice | Key validated evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Data source | GENECI's raw `lists/GRN_*.csv` | Pre-binarized `normalized_weight_matrix_*.csv` files invalidate any threshold sweep |
| Input topology | Top-10% per algorithm, rank-based | Fixed cutoffs vary 0.3%-67% density across algorithms at the same value; 10% ~ 2-3x true density |
| Node features | Identity matrix | Real expression as features tested and clearly worse |
| Encoder | 3-layer GCN, widths (32,32,16) | 2-layer, 4-layer, GraphSAGE, Jumping Knowledge, 4 alternative width shapes all tested, none won |
| Decoder | Bilinear + distance, averaged | Each alone beat plain inner-product; ensemble beat both individually on AUPR, all 3 networks |
| Fusion | Continuous averaging | ~0.02 AUROC gain over binarize-then-count, on identical trained models |
| Epochs | 300 | Every decoder alternative showed further gains beyond the original 150 |
| Final cutoff (optional) | Tukey's IQR rule, k depends on decoder | Near-oracle F1 achieved on plain decoder (k=3.0); bilinear needs looser k=1.5 |

# Things tested and rejected — full log

This is the most important section for avoiding wasted effort. Everything below was
implemented and empirically tested (not just considered), and did not make it into the
production pipeline. Re-testing any of these without new evidence would be repeating
already-done work.

| Idea | Result | Why rejected |
|---|---|---|
| Real gene expression as node features (replacing identity) | Clearly worse on all metrics | Identity lets GCN learn pure topology, which better matches the reconstruction task |
| Joint/shared encoder training across all algorithms (one model, not 17) | Inconclusive, roughly tied with independent training | Independent per-algorithm training holds its own; joint training needed more epochs just to reach parity |
| Correlation-weighted edges (expression correlation as edge-confidence multiplier) | No improvement | Tied or slightly worse than unweighted |
| "Native-weight" edge confidence (each algorithm's own raw score as edge weight, vs. binary presence) | Inconclusive on real continuous data | Initially looked promising, but that was on a pre-binarized file (invalid test); on real data, roughly a wash |
| Binarize-then-vote-count fusion (original method) | Beaten by continuous averaging | ~0.02 AUROC worse than continuous averaging, controlled test |
| Borda-count / rank-based fusion | Clearly worse | Discards confidence magnitude, keeps only rank order |
| Similarity Network Fusion (SNF) | Mixed trade-off (worse AUROC, better AUPR) | Not adopted as default; may be worth revisiting if AUPR is the only priority |
| NMF-based fusion, entropy-weighted fusion, Jaccard-based algorithm filtering | No improvement (tied with simple averaging) | -- |
| Entropy-weighted fusion + Jaccard-filtering combined | Catastrophic failure (AUROC ~0.61, near-random) | The entropy formula's actual math rewards single-algorithm-confident edges, not genuine cross-algorithm agreement -- contrary to its own inline documentation's stated intent |
| GAT (attention) encoder | Clearly worse, and ~67% slower | Each gene has too few neighbors at this topology density for attention to add value over uniform GCN averaging |
| GraphSAGE encoder (tested alone, and paired with bilinear decoder) | Clearly worse both times | -- |
| Jumping Knowledge (concatenating all 3 GCN layers before decoding) | Worse, and did not improve with more training | Genuine underperformer, not just undertrained |
| MLP decoder | Needed more epochs to show gains; eventually beat baseline AUPR at 450 epochs | Promising but never beat bilinear or the bilinear+distance ensemble; not adopted as primary |
| Focal Loss (gamma=2, alpha=0.25) | Mixed across networks -- won on 1, lost on 1, split on 1 | Not a consistent win |
| Hard-negative mining using the model's own confidence scores | Catastrophic failure (near-random on all networks) | Model was punished for confidently proposing real hidden links -- directly undermines the GCN's intended "discover hidden edges" behavior |
| Structural hard-negative mining (common-neighbors based, not model-score based) | Small positive signal on 1 network, clearly worse on 2 others | Does not generalize |
| Alternative encoder widths (funnel, wide-middle, bottleneck, constant-wide) | None beat (32,32,16) at any epoch count tested | -- |
| Deeper 4-layer width (32,32,16,8) | Clearly worse | Consistent with width-sweep finding that current shape is already good |
| Algorithm ablation (remove 3/6/9 of 16 algorithms, averaged over repeats) | Non-monotonic; going below 8 algorithms clearly hurts, but partial removal (down to ~10) is sometimes neutral or even slightly better | Confirms real redundancy exists among the 16, but doesn't cleanly prove "more is strictly always better" |
| Grouping/clustering redundant algorithms before fusion (hand-guessed methodology families, and real Jaccard-similarity-based unsupervised clustering) | Wash or slightly worse on both tested groupings | Flat averaging already implicitly handles redundancy reasonably well; explicit grouping removes reinforcement rather than fixing a real problem |
| Max (instead of mean) within algorithm groups | Clearly worse on all networks/metrics tested | Max is far more sensitive to single-algorithm noise spikes than mean |
| Top-20% or higher input topology density (re-tested specifically with the bilinear decoder) | Clearly worse, and gets worse the higher the density | The "5-20% stable" finding was specific to the old decoder and did not transfer; 10% is closer to the real peak for bilinear |

# Benchmark comparison

Comparison against the published GENECI benchmark table (best individual algorithm and
GENECI's own best evolutionary-optimized ensemble), same DREAM4 networks:

| Network | Best single algorithm | Best GENECI (their ensemble) | This pipeline (bilinear, no pruning) |
|---|---|---|---|
| D4_100_1 | GENIE3_ET: AUROC 0.7733, AUPR 0.0756 | AUROC 0.7623, AUPR 0.0676 | **AUROC 0.7975, AUPR 0.1073** |
| D4_100_2 | GENIE3_GBM: AUROC 0.6929, AUPR 0.0624 | AUROC 0.665, AUPR 0.0691 | **AUROC 0.6944 (narrow), AUPR 0.1025** (at 450 epochs) |
| D4_100_3 | GENIE3_RF: AUROC 0.7411, AUPR 0.1182 | AUROC 0.7396, AUPR 0.1265 | AUROC 0.7091 (below), **AUPR 0.1337** |

**Honest summary:** wins AUPR on all 3 networks tested (no exceptions) -- the priority
metric given the class imbalance in this problem. Wins AUROC on 2 of 3; GENIE3_RF
specifically holds a real AUROC edge on network 3. Not an unqualified sweep, but a
genuine, defensible result on the metric that matters most.

# Open items / not yet done

These are real, identified next steps, not vague ideas:

1. **E. coli / DREAM5 validation is the single highest-priority item.** Every result
   above is from the DREAM4 synthetic-network family. A real biological organism test
   (E. coli, DREAM5 Network 3, which has genuine curated regulatory ground truth via
   RegulonDB) is the actual test of whether any of this generalizes beyond DREAM4's
   specific synthetic quirks.
2. Whether the validated "2-3x expected density" input-topology multiplier transfers to
   E. coli's real density (computable from RegulonDB's documented TF-target statistics)
   is unverified.
3. Network 2 (of the 3 DREAM4 networks) consistently resisted almost every improvement
   that helped on networks 1 and 3 -- the underlying reason was never identified. Worth
   investigating if time allows, since it may reveal something structural about when
   this method does/doesn't work.
4. PPI-filtered high-order (2-hop) neighbor construction (inspired by a related published
   method, CaHoT-GRN) -- cannot be tested on DREAM4 (synthetic genes have no real protein
   identity to check against a PPI database), but is directly testable once E. coli data
   is available (STRING database), and would specifically test whether PPI-based
   filtering recovers genuine regulatory relationships or conflates them with general
   pathway co-membership -- a real, flagged concern, not yet resolved either way.
5. Tukey final-cutoff k value has only been tuned/checked against the plain decoder
   (k=3.0) and the bilinear decoder alone (k=1.5) -- never validated for the bilinear+
   distance ensemble output specifically.
6. A proper, formal held-out validation split (as opposed to the principled-but-informal
   validation approach used throughout, e.g. testing on multiple networks, using
   ground-truth-blind cutoff rules) has not been built. Recommended before any final
   paper-ready numbers are reported, to fully rule out any remaining leakage concerns.

# Existing reference implementations

Three working Python scripts already exist in `models/`, each a complete, runnable
pipeline (not just a sketch):

- **`gcn_gae_improved_model.py`** -- first validated version: real continuous data,
  top-X% input threshold, continuous-averaging fusion, plain inner-product decoder.
- **`gcn_gae_bilinear_model.py`** -- adds the bilinear decoder (single decoder, not yet
  the ensemble).
- **`gcn_gae_ensemble_best_model.py`** -- current best: bilinear + distance decoders,
  averaged together. This is the one to build the package around.

Each file's own docstring contains the same validated-choices reasoning as this
document, scoped to what that specific file implements.

# Suggested package structure (for the next development session)

A reasonable module breakdown, based on the pipeline's natural stages:

```
package_name/
  data/
    loaders.py        # load_algorithm_matrices() and related I/O
  topology/
    threshold.py       # top-X% rank-based edge construction
  models/
    encoders.py         # GCNEncoder (and any future alternatives)
    decoders.py         # BilinearDecoder, DistanceDecoder
  training/
    train.py            # train_gae(), iteration/epoch loop
  fusion/
    combine.py           # continuous averaging across algorithms/iterations/decoders
  postprocessing/
    tukey_cutoff.py       # optional final network extraction
  evaluation/
    metrics.py             # AUROC/AUPR/F1 helpers
  cli.py                    # command-line entry point, argument parsing
tests/
  (one test module per pipeline stage, using a small synthetic fixture dataset)
```

This mirrors the six pipeline steps above directly, which should make it straightforward
to hand each module's responsibility to a fresh development session with this document
as its full specification.
